medical.title: CBD oil offers no behavioral benefit for youths with intellectual disability, new study finds
medical.summary: Cannabis contains two key compounds that act on the brain: cannabidiol (CBD) and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). Although both interact with the body's endocannabinoid system, the outcomes of consuming them are poles apart. THC is the compound responsible for marijuana's intoxicating high and can sometimes trigger adverse effects, including psychosis. CBD, on the other hand, is associated with potential anxiety-relieving and anti-inflammatory effects. Despite limited evidence that it works, over the last decade, CBD-rich medical cannabis has gained popularity as a treatment for behavioral problems in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

medical.title: Video games may reduce rise in presurgery anxiety in children
medical.summary: A racing video game may seem out of place in the operating room, but it could help with presurgery anxiety. A study by Yale's Department of Anesthesiology published in the Journal of Clinical Anesthesia found that playing a driving-themed video game immediately before surgery may reduce the rise in presurgery anxiety in children ages 4 to 14. The children were undergoing procedures with general anesthesia.

medical.title: Boredom is closely related to poor sleep
medical.summary: We might think that boredom mainly affects us emotionally because it feels bad to be bored. But a new study expands boredom research by looking at sleep quality as an important factor related to boredom, linking it with impacts on our overall health, too.

medical.title: Brain model offers new explanation for memory formation and how dementia disrupts it
medical.summary: A new framework, published in Brain, could reshape researchers' understanding of how the brain creates memories and experiences, and how disruptions in this process may indicate Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.

medical.title: Freezing leftovers? Why some foods thaw well but others turn to goo
medical.summary: Bulk cooking and freezing your leftovers can be a great way to save money—while also reducing food waste and stocking your kitchen with convenient weeknight meals.

medical.title: Novel compound eases paralysis and activates nerve repair pathways in multiple sclerosis mouse model
medical.summary: A new derivative of a natural compound reduced symptoms associated with multiple sclerosis and promoted the central nervous system's regenerative pathways in a mouse model, report researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and collaborators at Keio University and Chiba University in Japan.

medical.title: With measles spreading, do you need a booster shot?
medical.summary: Now that measles is officially back in the U.S., some Americans are asking: Do adults need a booster shot?

medical.title: A vaccine for acne? Scientists are working on it
medical.summary: Acne affects around 85% of adolescents and can persist well into adulthood. For some, this means occasional pimples. For others, it can mean years of painful inflammation, scarring and lost confidence.

medical.title: AI-generated hospital discharge summaries earn higher clinical ratings than doctor-written versions
medical.summary: AI-generated discharge summaries can meet, and in some respects exceed, current standards of care, according to new research led by iCARE (Imperial Clinical Analytics, Research and Evaluation).

medical.title: How poetry can offer a vital, humane response to dementia
medical.summary: I'm sitting in the lounge of a Midlands nursing home on a hazy September morning. Most of the residents here have dementia and, as in many care and nursing homes, they lack meaningful ways to spend their time.

medical.title: Is my child eating enough? Fathers want more support when it comes to young children's eating habits
medical.summary: Getting young children to eat can be a source of both joy and worry. First-time fathers may feel unsure about how to manage their child's appetite and mealtimes, according to a study led by Ylva Törner Le Priol, a doctoral student at the Department of Food Studies, Nutrition and Dietetics at Uppsala University. The findings, published in PLOS One, point to a need for clearer and more practical support from child health services.

medical.title: Silencing a liver gene may prevent brain damage from rare metabolic disease
medical.summary: What if the path to treating a rare condition that harms the brain goes through the liver? A new study by Duke University School of Medicine researchers is the first to show preclinical success of a liver-targeting treatment of glutaric aciduria type I (GA1).

medical.title: When is a risk worth taking? Hunger helps the brain decide
medical.summary: Researchers have pinpointed a brain circuit in flies that brings together signals about hunger, food cues and danger to determine when animals take risks. The study published in Science Advances and led by Professor Carolina Rezaval and her research team at the University of Birmingham reveals how neural circuits integrate hunger, food cues and danger to guide behavioral choices.

medical.title: How a genetic growth brake helps control brain size—and what happens when it fails
medical.summary: The gene PTEN acts like a molecular brake. It helps maintain balance during brain development, when specific progenitor cells must be present at the right time, in the right place and in the right numbers.

medical.title: Wearable patch could help detect silent heart injury after surgery
medical.summary: Researchers at McMaster University have developed a wearable device that could help detect silent heart injury in the days after surgery, offering a new way to monitor patients after they leave the hospital.

medical.title: Researchers compare AI tools for analyzing tumor tissue
medical.summary: Researchers at Skoltech, the University of Sharjah in the United Arab Emirates and Tokai University in Japan, together with colleagues, have published an open-access review of computer vision in histopathology. The review examines how algorithms can identify tissue features in lung, breast, colorectal and prostate cancers.

medical.title: An mRNA booster for cellular immunotherapy shows potential against aggressive brain tumors
medical.summary: A team led by researchers at the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) and the University Medical Center Mannheim (UMM) has developed a new approach to more effectively direct immune cells against glioblastomas. In experimental models, they were able to show that a targeted mRNA vaccine significantly increases the potency of therapeutic immune cells. The paper is published in the journal Cancer Research.

medical.title: Lab-grown mini-guts offer a new way to study how the gut renews itself
medical.summary: Researchers have developed an expandable line of intestinal support cells that can help sustain miniature gut tissues in the laboratory without added growth factors. By making these normally scarce, difficult-to-grow cells available for repeated experiments, the team has created a new tool for studying the environment that maintains intestinal stem cells.

medical.title: Self-adjusting EEG helmet enables easy and reliable brainwave monitoring
medical.summary: A self-adjusting electroencephalography (EEG) monitoring helmet has been developed to enable easier and more reliable brainwave measurements in various fields, including clinical settings, rehabilitation and brain–computer interfaces (BCIs). The helmet monitors electrode–scalp contact conditions in real time and automatically adjusts electrode positions to maintain stable contact. By reducing measurement variability caused by differences in users' head shapes and hair conditions, the technology is expected to improve the reliability of EEG measurements.

medical.title: Dual-targeted CAR T-cell therapy shows promise in patients with treatment-resistant multiple myeloma
medical.summary: A first-in-human study by Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute investigators found that a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy called TriPRIL reduced or eliminated signs of cancer in 12 of 15 patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. TriPRIL—short for trimeric APRIL (a proliferation-inducing ligand)—recognizes two proteins on myeloma cells instead of just one. Researchers published their findings in The Lancet.

medical.title: Opening new grocery stores doesn't increase food access in low-income areas, research shows
medical.summary: Food deserts, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, are low-income neighborhoods where residents have limited access to healthy and affordable food. Opening a grocery store is a commonly proposed solution to improve food access in these areas, but that doesn't necessarily mean residents will shop there.

medical.title: Two studies in US veterans find updated COVID vaccines protect against severe illness
medical.summary: Two new studies involving more than 1 million U.S. veterans suggest that updated COVID-19 vaccines continue to provide meaningful protection against severe illness.

medical.title: Mental health crisis in children is real, say experts as cases soar fourfold
medical.summary: The number of children and teenagers seeking help for anxiety and depression has skyrocketed over the past two decades, and researchers say the rise cannot simply be dismissed as young people being more willing to talk about their feelings.

medical.title: 1 in 10 U.S. adults reported GLP-1 medication use July to August 2025
medical.summary: From July to August 2025, about one in 10 U.S. adults reported taking a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) medication during the past year, according to research published in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

medical.title: Study explores potential antiviral treatment approach for long COVID
medical.summary: Researchers have reported encouraging results from a new feasibility study looking to find a potential treatment for long COVID.

science.title: Insects on these sub‑Antarctic islands are bouncing back after invasive rats and mice were eradicated
science.summary: Island species typically evolve in isolation—and often without many predators. As a result, islands are home to high numbers of unique species.

science.title: Learning science one virtual escape room at a time
science.summary: Albert Einstein's ghost is trapped inside a science laboratory, and he needs help escaping. Fortunately, a group of seventh graders is up to the challenge.

science.title: In Antarctica's ice‑free areas, even footprints can damage rare microscopic ecosystems
science.summary: The usual advice for people visiting wilderness areas is to leave nothing but footprints. But as our new study shows, even footprints may disturb rare ecosystems in Antarctica and cause irreversible changes.

science.title: Electrified fabric captures phosphate for potential recovery from wastewater
science.summary: When rain falls on farmland, lawns and gardens, it can wash phosphate from fertilizers into nearby waterways, triggering harmful algal blooms that cloud lakes and rivers, release toxins and rob the water of oxygen needed to sustain aquatic life. Now, Northwestern University and Argonne National Laboratory researchers have developed a reusable electrode that captures phosphate from water in laboratory tests, potentially recovering a valuable, nonrenewable resource while reducing water pollution.

science.title: Using light to switch molecular states in the smallest of spaces
science.summary: What if light could be used not just to observe matter, but to actively reprogram it? Photochromic materials contain molecules that switch between distinct molecular states when exposed to different colors of light. This ability offers exciting possibilities for optical memory and light-controlled electronic devices. However, controlling these molecular changes within extremely small spaces remains challenging because conventional optics cannot focus light to dimensions much smaller than its wavelength.

science.title: A new life cycle assessment of polyethylene packaging and alternatives in the US and Europe
science.summary: A new research study assessed five major PE packaging applications and organized the analysis around three germane, current questions. How does PE compare with paper, glass, and metal alternatives? How do reuse, post-consumer recycled content, and end-of-life recycling affect the potential environmental impact results? What happens when package-level differences scale to projected demand through 2030 and beyond?

science.title: Migrating moth uses Earth's magnetic field as a compass
science.summary: Every year, the bogong moth sets off on long migrations through the night. To find its way, it uses the stars as a guide. Now, a new study from Lund University shows that, like migratory birds, the moth also has a built-in magnetic compass that helps it stay on course.

science.title: Crystal layers just 10 nanometers thick assemble into a tiny tunable grid
science.summary: Researchers have fabricated two ultrathin crystal sheets that, when stacked and rotated relative to each other, create a square lattice of defects at their interface. These defects change how electrical charges are arranged, and when the 10-nanometer-thick sheets are bonded and twisted, tiny electrical patterns emerge at the interface. These controllable arrangements could eventually prove useful in the electronics industry, although using them in a working device will require further research.

science.title: Inflated receipts and fake loans: Giving to charities to evade tax
science.summary: Some taxpayers use charitable donations to illegally reduce their taxes, using schemes orchestrated by promoters and supported by financial advisers and charities.

science.title: Physicists send an unblockable message using gravity
science.summary: University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter. The unusual experiment took place in UQ's Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between two levels, moving its 1.8 metric ton (4,000 pound) counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1.

science.title: MAF EAP – Holidays – How to manage the BAH HUMBUG that tries to sneak in
science.summary: Holidays are often a fun break during a busy year – a long weekend here and there is an event many of us can get behind.  However, when a short holiday break turns into a full holiday season, we know that this is a different “ball game”. Everyone has stress about something – some people […]

science.title: Water purification method turns old batteries into magnetic pollutant traps
science.summary: How can harmful substances be removed from water? When it comes to dyes that cannot simply be filtered out, this is usually very laborious: You need substances to which the dyes attach, and then the water often has to be painstakingly centrifuged.

science.title: How cells use alternative genetic instructions to produce 'shadowing proteins'
science.summary: The human genome contains tens of thousands of genes that provide instructions for making the proteins responsible for carrying out essential functions throughout the body. But those instructions may be more versatile than scientists once understood.

science.title: Researchers review isotope methods for tracing and quantifying gaseous nitrogen production in soils
science.summary: Researchers from the Institute of Applied Ecology (IAE) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have reviewed stable nitrogen isotope techniques for tracing the sources and quantifying the production of gaseous nitrogen in soils. The review examines four approaches for distinguishing microbial pathways that produce nitrous oxide (N₂O), nitric oxide (NO) and dinitrogen (N₂).

science.title: NASA Announces Mid-Power Electric Rocket Challenge for US Companies
science.summary: NASA launched a new competition inviting U.S. companies to produce prototypes of mid-power Hall effect thrusters – a type of electric propulsion system considered crucial for future space operations and exploration. Hall effect thrusters use an electric field to accelerate a propellant gas, producing efficient thrust for long-duration missions. Used for propelling satellites and deep […]

science.title: Bolivia's Madidi National Park shelters 99 bat species, including 7 new to the country
science.summary: A new study has confirmed 100 bat taxa in Madidi National Park, in northwestern Bolivia, including 99 recognized species and one that may be new to science. The park is home to 68% of the bat species known from Bolivia.

science.title: Making diversity count: New paper highlights overlooked scientists in the chemical sciences curriculum
science.summary: A new paper by James Wilton-Ely, Ravi Singh and collaborators explores how curriculum diversification can help address the underrepresentation of minority-background scientists in chemical sciences education.

science.title: Empire State Building Goes Gold for Voyager
science.summary: The Empire State Building is seen illuminated in gold to celebrate NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft as it was about to pass one light-day away from Earth, a distance reached by no other human-made object, Nov. 17, 2026. The color gold represents the gold-plated copper phonograph record that is flying on Voyager; the Golden Record contains […]

science.title: Bee-lieve it or not, bumblebees have a sweet spot for salt
science.summary: Minerals are vital for bumblebee health, but too much can be harmful. For this new study, which is published in Royal Society Open Science, researchers tested how buff-tailed bumblebees (Bombus terrestris) responded to different levels of calcium, potassium, magnesium and sodium in artificial nectar.

science.title: What Is the Moon Base?
science.summary: This article is for students. NASA is returning astronauts to the Moon – and this time they will spend more time on the lunar surface. The Moon Base is humanity’s first lunar outpost. It will be a place where astronauts live, work, and explore. ______________________________________________________________________ Words to Know outpost: a station or base located in […]

science.title: Thank You for Doing NASA Science!
science.summary: It’s Thanksgiving time, and we’re giving thanks to you for doing NASA Science with us! You and NASA’s other volunteers have enabled an incredible banquet of discoveries—by taking data, analyzing data, writing code, writing papers, and even inventing your own science projects. Whether you’re an expert participant or someone who’s just started your science journey, […]

science.title: Writing changes language less than we think
science.summary: Writing is one of the most important inventions in human history. It transformed how we share knowledge, communicate and pass information from one generation to the next. But has it also changed the way we build sentences and the complexity of our languages?

science.title: Miniaturization found at the origin of amphibians opens new ecological territory
science.summary: Frogs, salamanders and caecilians—the three groups of living amphibians—together number more than 9,000 species. On average, they are the smallest of all four-limbed vertebrates, and some are extremely small: Brachycephalus toads measure less than 7 millimeters (0.28 inches) from snout to vent. Their ancient relatives were very different animals. Most temnospondyls, the extinct group from which modern amphibians (lissamphibians) arose, were aquatic or semiaquatic predators 1 to 5 meters (3.3 to 16.4 feet) long.

science.title: How old is that puggle? Scientists develop first X-ray aging guide for echidnas
science.summary: A collaboration between Murdoch University researchers and veterinarians at Taronga Zoo has produced the first detailed radiographic aging guide for short-beaked echidnas, providing a practical new way to estimate the age of these iconic Australian mammals from the time they are tiny puggles through to early adulthood.

science.title: Parents feel judged as their child transitions from high school to adulthood
science.summary: Parenting a teenager can be difficult at times, and this can be compounded by the intense pressure some parents feel to ensure they are successfully guiding their child through their high school graduation to the next stage of their life.

environment.title: Payment scheme for human-wildlife coexistence faces growing criticism from Sámi reindeer herders
environment.summary: A Swedish compensation scheme designed to encourage coexistence between reindeer herders and carnivores is facing growing criticism from Indigenous Sámi communities. Inadequate payments, deficient monitoring methods and lack of meaningful dialogue between authorities and reindeer herders are eroding trust in the system, researchers tell Mongabay. “The state of Sweden hasn’t actually understood how severe and […]

environment.title: Francophone leaders must support jailed Mother Nature Cambodia activists (commentary)
environment.summary: Readers are certainly familiar with the Mother Nature Cambodia 5 (MNC5) after Mongabay released its documentary The Clearing in July 2025, chronicling the hopes, activism, and commitment of the group. The film detailed their lives while free on bail awaiting a likely guilty verdict for “plotting against the government” by fighting to protect Cambodia’s natural […]

environment.title: Rising preterm births in Bangladesh linked to extreme heat, research suggests
environment.summary: Hafsa Begum, 25, spent most of her recent pregnancy in a two-room apartment on the third floor of a five-storey building in a densely populated neighborhood of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Her bedroom remained dark even during the day, she says, as neighboring residential buildings blocked sunlight and restricted the flow of fresh air through the windows. […]

environment.title: Fossil of extinct giant bird discovered in Flores cave, Indonesia
environment.summary: Archaeologists excavating Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores have identified a new species of extinct giant bird that roamed the region some 150,000 years ago, according to a recent study. The giant bird was a kind of megapode — large, chicken-like birds that today live in the broader Australasian region. These birds […]

environment.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

environment.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
environment.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

environment.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
environment.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

environment.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

environment.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

environment.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
environment.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

mix_items.summary: Europarlamentara Diana Şoşoacă e foc şi pară de când a aflat că ucrainenii au distrus cu dronele podul care leagă… The post Din solidaritate cu podul ruşilor, Şoşoacă încearcă de ore întregi să dărâme Pasajul Basarab appeared first on Times New Roman .

mix_items.title: CBD oil offers no behavioral benefit for youths with intellectual disability, new study finds
mix_items.summary: Cannabis contains two key compounds that act on the brain: cannabidiol (CBD) and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). Although both interact with the body's endocannabinoid system, the outcomes of consuming them are poles apart. THC is the compound responsible for marijuana's intoxicating high and can sometimes trigger adverse effects, including psychosis. CBD, on the other hand, is associated with potential anxiety-relieving and anti-inflammatory effects. Despite limited evidence that it works, over the last decade, CBD-rich medical cannabis has gained popularity as a treatment for behavioral problems in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

mix_items.title: Insects on these sub‑Antarctic islands are bouncing back after invasive rats and mice were eradicated
mix_items.summary: Island species typically evolve in isolation—and often without many predators. As a result, islands are home to high numbers of unique species.

mix_items.title: Learning science one virtual escape room at a time
mix_items.summary: Albert Einstein's ghost is trapped inside a science laboratory, and he needs help escaping. Fortunately, a group of seventh graders is up to the challenge.

mix_items.title: Video games may reduce rise in presurgery anxiety in children
mix_items.summary: A racing video game may seem out of place in the operating room, but it could help with presurgery anxiety. A study by Yale's Department of Anesthesiology published in the Journal of Clinical Anesthesia found that playing a driving-themed video game immediately before surgery may reduce the rise in presurgery anxiety in children ages 4 to 14. The children were undergoing procedures with general anesthesia.

mix_items.title: In Antarctica's ice‑free areas, even footprints can damage rare microscopic ecosystems
mix_items.summary: The usual advice for people visiting wilderness areas is to leave nothing but footprints. But as our new study shows, even footprints may disturb rare ecosystems in Antarctica and cause irreversible changes.

mix_items.title: Boredom is closely related to poor sleep
mix_items.summary: We might think that boredom mainly affects us emotionally because it feels bad to be bored. But a new study expands boredom research by looking at sleep quality as an important factor related to boredom, linking it with impacts on our overall health, too.

mix_items.title: Electrified fabric captures phosphate for potential recovery from wastewater
mix_items.summary: When rain falls on farmland, lawns and gardens, it can wash phosphate from fertilizers into nearby waterways, triggering harmful algal blooms that cloud lakes and rivers, release toxins and rob the water of oxygen needed to sustain aquatic life. Now, Northwestern University and Argonne National Laboratory researchers have developed a reusable electrode that captures phosphate from water in laboratory tests, potentially recovering a valuable, nonrenewable resource while reducing water pollution.

mix_items.title: Brain model offers new explanation for memory formation and how dementia disrupts it
mix_items.summary: A new framework, published in Brain, could reshape researchers' understanding of how the brain creates memories and experiences, and how disruptions in this process may indicate Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.

mix_items.title: Freezing leftovers? Why some foods thaw well but others turn to goo
mix_items.summary: Bulk cooking and freezing your leftovers can be a great way to save money—while also reducing food waste and stocking your kitchen with convenient weeknight meals.

mix_items.title: Novel compound eases paralysis and activates nerve repair pathways in multiple sclerosis mouse model
mix_items.summary: A new derivative of a natural compound reduced symptoms associated with multiple sclerosis and promoted the central nervous system's regenerative pathways in a mouse model, report researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and collaborators at Keio University and Chiba University in Japan.

mix_items.title: Using light to switch molecular states in the smallest of spaces
mix_items.summary: What if light could be used not just to observe matter, but to actively reprogram it? Photochromic materials contain molecules that switch between distinct molecular states when exposed to different colors of light. This ability offers exciting possibilities for optical memory and light-controlled electronic devices. However, controlling these molecular changes within extremely small spaces remains challenging because conventional optics cannot focus light to dimensions much smaller than its wavelength.

mix_items.title: A new life cycle assessment of polyethylene packaging and alternatives in the US and Europe
mix_items.summary: A new research study assessed five major PE packaging applications and organized the analysis around three germane, current questions. How does PE compare with paper, glass, and metal alternatives? How do reuse, post-consumer recycled content, and end-of-life recycling affect the potential environmental impact results? What happens when package-level differences scale to projected demand through 2030 and beyond?

mix_items.title: With measles spreading, do you need a booster shot?
mix_items.summary: Now that measles is officially back in the U.S., some Americans are asking: Do adults need a booster shot?

mix_items.title: A vaccine for acne? Scientists are working on it
mix_items.summary: Acne affects around 85% of adolescents and can persist well into adulthood. For some, this means occasional pimples. For others, it can mean years of painful inflammation, scarring and lost confidence.

mix_items.title: AI-generated hospital discharge summaries earn higher clinical ratings than doctor-written versions
mix_items.summary: AI-generated discharge summaries can meet, and in some respects exceed, current standards of care, according to new research led by iCARE (Imperial Clinical Analytics, Research and Evaluation).

mix_items.title: Migrating moth uses Earth's magnetic field as a compass
mix_items.summary: Every year, the bogong moth sets off on long migrations through the night. To find its way, it uses the stars as a guide. Now, a new study from Lund University shows that, like migratory birds, the moth also has a built-in magnetic compass that helps it stay on course.

mix_items.title: Crystal layers just 10 nanometers thick assemble into a tiny tunable grid
mix_items.summary: Researchers have fabricated two ultrathin crystal sheets that, when stacked and rotated relative to each other, create a square lattice of defects at their interface. These defects change how electrical charges are arranged, and when the 10-nanometer-thick sheets are bonded and twisted, tiny electrical patterns emerge at the interface. These controllable arrangements could eventually prove useful in the electronics industry, although using them in a working device will require further research.

mix_items.title: Inflated receipts and fake loans: Giving to charities to evade tax
mix_items.summary: Some taxpayers use charitable donations to illegally reduce their taxes, using schemes orchestrated by promoters and supported by financial advisers and charities.

mix_items.title: How poetry can offer a vital, humane response to dementia
mix_items.summary: I'm sitting in the lounge of a Midlands nursing home on a hazy September morning. Most of the residents here have dementia and, as in many care and nursing homes, they lack meaningful ways to spend their time.

mix_items.title: Physicists send an unblockable message using gravity
mix_items.summary: University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter. The unusual experiment took place in UQ's Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between two levels, moving its 1.8 metric ton (4,000 pound) counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1.

mix_items.title: Is my child eating enough? Fathers want more support when it comes to young children's eating habits
mix_items.summary: Getting young children to eat can be a source of both joy and worry. First-time fathers may feel unsure about how to manage their child's appetite and mealtimes, according to a study led by Ylva Törner Le Priol, a doctoral student at the Department of Food Studies, Nutrition and Dietetics at Uppsala University. The findings, published in PLOS One, point to a need for clearer and more practical support from child health services.

mix_items.title: Silencing a liver gene may prevent brain damage from rare metabolic disease
mix_items.summary: What if the path to treating a rare condition that harms the brain goes through the liver? A new study by Duke University School of Medicine researchers is the first to show preclinical success of a liver-targeting treatment of glutaric aciduria type I (GA1).

mix_items.title: When is a risk worth taking? Hunger helps the brain decide
mix_items.summary: Researchers have pinpointed a brain circuit in flies that brings together signals about hunger, food cues and danger to determine when animals take risks. The study published in Science Advances and led by Professor Carolina Rezaval and her research team at the University of Birmingham reveals how neural circuits integrate hunger, food cues and danger to guide behavioral choices.

mix_items.title: How a genetic growth brake helps control brain size—and what happens when it fails
mix_items.summary: The gene PTEN acts like a molecular brake. It helps maintain balance during brain development, when specific progenitor cells must be present at the right time, in the right place and in the right numbers.

mix_items.title: Wearable patch could help detect silent heart injury after surgery
mix_items.summary: Researchers at McMaster University have developed a wearable device that could help detect silent heart injury in the days after surgery, offering a new way to monitor patients after they leave the hospital.

mix_items.title: MAF EAP – Holidays – How to manage the BAH HUMBUG that tries to sneak in
mix_items.summary: Holidays are often a fun break during a busy year – a long weekend here and there is an event many of us can get behind.  However, when a short holiday break turns into a full holiday season, we know that this is a different “ball game”. Everyone has stress about something – some people […]

mix_items.title: Water purification method turns old batteries into magnetic pollutant traps
mix_items.summary: How can harmful substances be removed from water? When it comes to dyes that cannot simply be filtered out, this is usually very laborious: You need substances to which the dyes attach, and then the water often has to be painstakingly centrifuged.

mix_items.title: How cells use alternative genetic instructions to produce 'shadowing proteins'
mix_items.summary: The human genome contains tens of thousands of genes that provide instructions for making the proteins responsible for carrying out essential functions throughout the body. But those instructions may be more versatile than scientists once understood.

mix_items.title: Researchers review isotope methods for tracing and quantifying gaseous nitrogen production in soils
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the Institute of Applied Ecology (IAE) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have reviewed stable nitrogen isotope techniques for tracing the sources and quantifying the production of gaseous nitrogen in soils. The review examines four approaches for distinguishing microbial pathways that produce nitrous oxide (N₂O), nitric oxide (NO) and dinitrogen (N₂).

mix_items.title: Researchers compare AI tools for analyzing tumor tissue
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Skoltech, the University of Sharjah in the United Arab Emirates and Tokai University in Japan, together with colleagues, have published an open-access review of computer vision in histopathology. The review examines how algorithms can identify tissue features in lung, breast, colorectal and prostate cancers.

mix_items.title: An mRNA booster for cellular immunotherapy shows potential against aggressive brain tumors
mix_items.summary: A team led by researchers at the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) and the University Medical Center Mannheim (UMM) has developed a new approach to more effectively direct immune cells against glioblastomas. In experimental models, they were able to show that a targeted mRNA vaccine significantly increases the potency of therapeutic immune cells. The paper is published in the journal Cancer Research.

mix_items.title: NASA Announces Mid-Power Electric Rocket Challenge for US Companies
mix_items.summary: NASA launched a new competition inviting U.S. companies to produce prototypes of mid-power Hall effect thrusters – a type of electric propulsion system considered crucial for future space operations and exploration. Hall effect thrusters use an electric field to accelerate a propellant gas, producing efficient thrust for long-duration missions. Used for propelling satellites and deep […]

mix_items.title: Bolivia's Madidi National Park shelters 99 bat species, including 7 new to the country
mix_items.summary: A new study has confirmed 100 bat taxa in Madidi National Park, in northwestern Bolivia, including 99 recognized species and one that may be new to science. The park is home to 68% of the bat species known from Bolivia.

mix_items.title: Making diversity count: New paper highlights overlooked scientists in the chemical sciences curriculum
mix_items.summary: A new paper by James Wilton-Ely, Ravi Singh and collaborators explores how curriculum diversification can help address the underrepresentation of minority-background scientists in chemical sciences education.

mix_items.title: Lab-grown mini-guts offer a new way to study how the gut renews itself
mix_items.summary: Researchers have developed an expandable line of intestinal support cells that can help sustain miniature gut tissues in the laboratory without added growth factors. By making these normally scarce, difficult-to-grow cells available for repeated experiments, the team has created a new tool for studying the environment that maintains intestinal stem cells.

mix_items.title: Empire State Building Goes Gold for Voyager
mix_items.summary: The Empire State Building is seen illuminated in gold to celebrate NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft as it was about to pass one light-day away from Earth, a distance reached by no other human-made object, Nov. 17, 2026. The color gold represents the gold-plated copper phonograph record that is flying on Voyager; the Golden Record contains […]

mix_items.title: Self-adjusting EEG helmet enables easy and reliable brainwave monitoring
mix_items.summary: A self-adjusting electroencephalography (EEG) monitoring helmet has been developed to enable easier and more reliable brainwave measurements in various fields, including clinical settings, rehabilitation and brain–computer interfaces (BCIs). The helmet monitors electrode–scalp contact conditions in real time and automatically adjusts electrode positions to maintain stable contact. By reducing measurement variability caused by differences in users' head shapes and hair conditions, the technology is expected to improve the reliability of EEG measurements.

mix_items.title: Dual-targeted CAR T-cell therapy shows promise in patients with treatment-resistant multiple myeloma
mix_items.summary: A first-in-human study by Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute investigators found that a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy called TriPRIL reduced or eliminated signs of cancer in 12 of 15 patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. TriPRIL—short for trimeric APRIL (a proliferation-inducing ligand)—recognizes two proteins on myeloma cells instead of just one. Researchers published their findings in The Lancet.

mix_items.title: Bee-lieve it or not, bumblebees have a sweet spot for salt
mix_items.summary: Minerals are vital for bumblebee health, but too much can be harmful. For this new study, which is published in Royal Society Open Science, researchers tested how buff-tailed bumblebees (Bombus terrestris) responded to different levels of calcium, potassium, magnesium and sodium in artificial nectar.

mix_items.title: What Is the Moon Base?
mix_items.summary: This article is for students. NASA is returning astronauts to the Moon – and this time they will spend more time on the lunar surface. The Moon Base is humanity’s first lunar outpost. It will be a place where astronauts live, work, and explore. ______________________________________________________________________ Words to Know outpost: a station or base located in […]

mix_items.title: Thank You for Doing NASA Science!
mix_items.summary: It’s Thanksgiving time, and we’re giving thanks to you for doing NASA Science with us! You and NASA’s other volunteers have enabled an incredible banquet of discoveries—by taking data, analyzing data, writing code, writing papers, and even inventing your own science projects. Whether you’re an expert participant or someone who’s just started your science journey, […]

mix_items.title: Writing changes language less than we think
mix_items.summary: Writing is one of the most important inventions in human history. It transformed how we share knowledge, communicate and pass information from one generation to the next. But has it also changed the way we build sentences and the complexity of our languages?

mix_items.title: Opening new grocery stores doesn't increase food access in low-income areas, research shows
mix_items.summary: Food deserts, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, are low-income neighborhoods where residents have limited access to healthy and affordable food. Opening a grocery store is a commonly proposed solution to improve food access in these areas, but that doesn't necessarily mean residents will shop there.

mix_items.title: Miniaturization found at the origin of amphibians opens new ecological territory
mix_items.summary: Frogs, salamanders and caecilians—the three groups of living amphibians—together number more than 9,000 species. On average, they are the smallest of all four-limbed vertebrates, and some are extremely small: Brachycephalus toads measure less than 7 millimeters (0.28 inches) from snout to vent. Their ancient relatives were very different animals. Most temnospondyls, the extinct group from which modern amphibians (lissamphibians) arose, were aquatic or semiaquatic predators 1 to 5 meters (3.3 to 16.4 feet) long.

mix_items.title: Two studies in US veterans find updated COVID vaccines protect against severe illness
mix_items.summary: Two new studies involving more than 1 million U.S. veterans suggest that updated COVID-19 vaccines continue to provide meaningful protection against severe illness.

mix_items.title: Mental health crisis in children is real, say experts as cases soar fourfold
mix_items.summary: The number of children and teenagers seeking help for anxiety and depression has skyrocketed over the past two decades, and researchers say the rise cannot simply be dismissed as young people being more willing to talk about their feelings.

mix_items.title: 1 in 10 U.S. adults reported GLP-1 medication use July to August 2025
mix_items.summary: From July to August 2025, about one in 10 U.S. adults reported taking a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) medication during the past year, according to research published in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

mix_items.title: How old is that puggle? Scientists develop first X-ray aging guide for echidnas
mix_items.summary: A collaboration between Murdoch University researchers and veterinarians at Taronga Zoo has produced the first detailed radiographic aging guide for short-beaked echidnas, providing a practical new way to estimate the age of these iconic Australian mammals from the time they are tiny puggles through to early adulthood.

mix_items.title: Study explores potential antiviral treatment approach for long COVID
mix_items.summary: Researchers have reported encouraging results from a new feasibility study looking to find a potential treatment for long COVID.

mix_items.title: Parents feel judged as their child transitions from high school to adulthood
mix_items.summary: Parenting a teenager can be difficult at times, and this can be compounded by the intense pressure some parents feel to ensure they are successfully guiding their child through their high school graduation to the next stage of their life.

mix_items.title: Payment scheme for human-wildlife coexistence faces growing criticism from Sámi reindeer herders
mix_items.summary: A Swedish compensation scheme designed to encourage coexistence between reindeer herders and carnivores is facing growing criticism from Indigenous Sámi communities. Inadequate payments, deficient monitoring methods and lack of meaningful dialogue between authorities and reindeer herders are eroding trust in the system, researchers tell Mongabay. “The state of Sweden hasn’t actually understood how severe and […]

mix_items.title: Francophone leaders must support jailed Mother Nature Cambodia activists (commentary)
mix_items.summary: Readers are certainly familiar with the Mother Nature Cambodia 5 (MNC5) after Mongabay released its documentary The Clearing in July 2025, chronicling the hopes, activism, and commitment of the group. The film detailed their lives while free on bail awaiting a likely guilty verdict for “plotting against the government” by fighting to protect Cambodia’s natural […]

mix_items.title: Rising preterm births in Bangladesh linked to extreme heat, research suggests
mix_items.summary: Hafsa Begum, 25, spent most of her recent pregnancy in a two-room apartment on the third floor of a five-storey building in a densely populated neighborhood of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Her bedroom remained dark even during the day, she says, as neighboring residential buildings blocked sunlight and restricted the flow of fresh air through the windows. […]

mix_items.title: Fossil of extinct giant bird discovered in Flores cave, Indonesia
mix_items.summary: Archaeologists excavating Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores have identified a new species of extinct giant bird that roamed the region some 150,000 years ago, according to a recent study. The giant bird was a kind of megapode — large, chicken-like birds that today live in the broader Australasian region. These birds […]

mix_items.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

mix_items.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
mix_items.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

mix_items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
mix_items.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

mix_items.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

mix_items.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
mix_items.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.
